items.title: SpaceXAI has released Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 today, with the High reasoning variant debuting at #...
items.content:
SpaceXAI has released Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 today, with the High reasoning variant debuting at #2 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 82.9%, and #1 on Tau Voice for Agentic Performance at 56.5% - among the fastest models at 0.70s Time to First Audio

Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 is SpaceXAI's successor to Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0 (75.7% on the Speech to Speech Index). It is the only model in the Index's top five with an average Time to First Audio under 1 second, achieving 0.70 seconds vs. 1.14 seconds for the next fastest, GPT-Realtime-2 High.

Key takeaways:
➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High debuts at #2 at 82.9%, only behind Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus (84.1%) and ahead of GPT-Realtime-2.1 High (79.1%) and GPT-Realtime-2 High (77.2%). This is up 7.3 percentage points from Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0 (75.7%)
➤ Speech to Speech Index by Benchmark: On Tau Voice, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High is the new leader at 56.5%, just ahead of Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 54.6% and its predecessor Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0 at 52.1%. On Big Bench Audio, it achieves 97.2%, behind leader Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 99.2%. On our Full Duplex Bench subset, it scores 95.1%, up from 77.8% for Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0, the largest driver of its index gain, behind Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 98.4%
➤ Speed: The model’s average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.70 seconds, faster than GPT-Realtime-2 High (1.14s), GPT-Realtime-2.1 High (1.21s), and Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0 (1.25s), and well ahead of Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus (4.02s)
➤ Price: Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 is priced at $4.80 per hour of input audio, up from $3.00 for Grok Voice Think Fast 1.0 and more expensive than Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus ($4.42) and GPT-Realtime-2 High ($4.14), but ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High ($10.75)

Congratulations @SpaceXAI @elonmusk! See below for more detail ⬇️

items.content:
This post on Anthropic by @dkthomp sounds compelling but I don’t think it actually is.

1. The projections of Anthropic’s revenue are likely overoptimistic. Their big Q2 was projected to be $10.9B (after $4.8B in Q1) but importantly that was at the height of tokenmaxxing, and before strong new competition from Chinese models like Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2, and at moment, now perhaps over, when they were media darlings.  I really don’t see them getting to $100B+ for the year with $85B+ to go, given the new headwinds. 

2. Not really fair to compare to Elon’s companies, which actually aren’t wildly impressive on revenue. Only Tesla is even in the top 100. Even if Anthropic’s revenue *was* $150B, that still would NOT put them in the top 25 US companies by revenue [https://t.co/85bu9d3jaA]. So I find framing the comparison in terms of Elon’s net worth (mostly based on speculation about the future) to be a bit misleading. 

3. The real long-term question is about profits. Anthropic’s best quarter was Q2 of this year, but that relied on a big one-time subsidy for Elon, and again was at the height of tokenmaxxing and before the sharpest Chinese competition. In every other quarter they lost money and it’s not at clear how Q3 will turn out.

items.title: The same knowledge in an LLM can support useful work, such as vaccine research, and harmful work, su...
items.content:
The same knowledge in an LLM can support useful work, such as vaccine research, and harmful work, such as biological weapons, yet training a separate model for every level of access is too expensive.

The authors of this paper introduce gradient-routed auxiliary modules, or GRAM: small parts added to a transformer whose parameters receive backpropagation updates only for selected kinds of training data, so specialized knowledge is encouraged to settle in a removable module rather than spread through the whole network.

Turning off a module at inference time then reduces the corresponding capability while leaving general performance largely intact.

The experiments move beyond a toy setting to virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and specialized code, compare the method with data filtering and model unlearning, and study models from 50 million to 5 billion parameters; GRAM stays close to the stronger but much more expensive data-filtering approach and resists recovery of removed capabilities after limited finetuning.

items.content:
My agent can now talk to your agent.

I'll have to take some time to think about the implications here.

Up to this point, your personal assistant agent, whether it's Hermes, OpenClaw, or something else, only knew you. It had no way to find someone else's agent and work something out directly.

This changes now.

The guys at BAND released an interaction layer for personal agents, enabling them to connect and work together.

BAND handles the identity, channels, routing, and delivery between agents.

Imagine you want to get dinner with a friend next week.

Instead of emailing back and forth trying to pick the perfect day, you tell your agent to sort it out using BAND.

1. Your agent checks your calendar and finds your free evenings
2. It messages your friend's agent in a shared channel
3. Their agent checks their calendar
4. It sends back the nights that overlap
5. Both agents agree on a night and a time
6. Your agent asks you before it books

Every collaboration is a channel. You pick who's in it, and limit the context each agent receives.

Every agent declares its capabilities up front, so requests are routed to the agent that can actually handle them. Everything is logged, so you can check what happened.

items.content:
Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over.

Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price.

We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times.

> One switch cost 11x warm
> Routing somewhere else cost 47% more
> Caches don't transfer between models

Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another.

The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt.

So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%.

Which part owns the decision on which model to use?,
When will a switch ever become profitable?,
And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?

items.content:
If you think that IoT maturity is about adding more devices, you are missing the real shift.

Edge AI and Swarm IoT bring intelligence closer to operations, where systems can coordinate before cloud delay weakens the response. 

Microblog by @antgrasso  about  #EdgeAI  #SwarmIoT

The point is not to connect more objects for the sake of collecting more data.

Edge AI and Swarm IoT make IoT more useful when connected systems can understand what is happening near the source and help operations respond sooner.

Edge AI supports this shift because some decisions should not wait for every signal to travel back to the cloud.

When data is processed near a machine or sensor, teams can act with less delay and less dependence on constant connectivity.

Swarm IoT adds coordination.

Devices do not only report status; they share signals and adjust behavior as a group.

This is where distributed assets start to work more like an operational network than a set of isolated endpoints.

The human role remains essential.

Leaders need clear governance and safety rules, so local intelligence stays aligned with business goals and does not become uncontrolled automation at the edge.

IoT maturity is not measured by the number of connected devices.

It is measured by how well intelligence and oversight work together where operations actually happen.
